title: Crowdsourcing a Word–Emotion Association Lexicon
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of building a large, high-quality lexicon of word–emotion and word–polarity associations, which was seen as a bottleneck for emotion analysis in natural language processing. The authors argue that existing emotion lexicons were small, costly to create, and limited in coverage, so they propose a crowdsourcing-based annotation approach using Amazon Mechanical Turk.

The intervention studied is not an educational intervention, but a crowdsourced annotation workflow. The authors designed mechanisms to improve annotation quality, including a preliminary word-choice question to guide annotators to the intended word sense and to filter out people unfamiliar with the term, plus careful question phrasing and automatic post-processing to remove low-quality assignments. They compared asking whether a word is "associated with" an emotion versus whether it "evokes" an emotion, and found the associated phrasing produced better inter-annotator agreement.

The study used English word and phrase targets drawn from the Macquarie Thesaurus, General Inquirer, and WordNet Affect Lexicon. Annotators on Mechanical Turk, who were required to be native or fluent English speakers, provided emotion ratings for eight basic emotions from Plutchik’s model. After filtering, the authors produced EmoLex, a lexicon of 8,883 terms with validated emotion associations. The main conclusion is that crowdsourcing can efficiently generate a large emotion lexicon with acceptable agreement when quality-control mechanisms are built into the task design.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a crowdsourced lexicon-creation and annotation methodology study, not an educational intervention study. It does not evaluate an AI tutoring, learning, or school-based system in K-12 settings.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured impact on learner outcomes, teacher workload, or K-12 institutional outcomes. The paper’s contributions are methodological for sentiment/emotion lexicon construction, with only a brief mention of tutoring as a potential downstream application.
